coverage.name: Hip drive out of the bottom
Heels flat on the floor
coverage.reason: Heel landmarks are frequently occluded by the far leg and by footwear, and a few pixels of rise is within noise. Reported at reduced confidence, and `cannot_assess` when the foot is occluded.

coverage.name: Bar placement on the back
coverage.reason: We can distinguish grossly high bar placement from plausible placement, and nothing finer. Never returns a confident "meets standard"; at best "consistent with low-bar placement".

coverage.name: Eye gaze direction
coverage.reason: Gaze is not observable; head orientation is. The head is also routinely occluded by the plate in a side view - it is in the common sample. Reports only a clear upward-directed head, otherwise `cannot_assess`.

coverage.name: Knees shoved out
coverage.reason: Knees-out is displacement in the frontal plane, perpendicular to the camera. A sagittal view contains no information about it. Requires a front or 45-degree camera.

coverage.name: Stance width and toe angle
coverage.reason: Stance width is a frontal-plane measurement and toe angle is a transverse-plane measurement. Neither is recoverable from a single sagittal view. The document's own illustration of the standard (Figure 2-12) is an overhead view.
coverage.needed: A front or overhead camera angle.

coverage.name: Rack height and unracking procedure
coverage.reason: A property of the setup before the set, not of a repetition. The rack and the unracking are typically outside the frame of an uploaded squat clip, and our analysis is rep-scoped.
coverage.needed: Footage of the unrack, with the rack uprights and the lifter both in frame.

detail.note: Positive means the hip landmark is below the knee landmark.

findings.reason: The hip finished within 0.03 shin-lengths of the knee (+0.019), which is inside our measurement tolerance. Depth is too close to call from this footage rather than clearly good or clearly short.
findings.quote: Correctly is deep, with hips dropping below level with the top of the patellas. Correctly is therefore full range of motion.
findings.feedback_source: Any squat that is not deep is a partial squat. If you are high, check that your stance is wide enough but not too wide, that your toes are out enough, and that your knees are tracking parallel to your feet - most people who squat high do not shove their knees out enough.
findings.uncertainty: The measurement is very close to the threshold, making it unclear whether depth reaches the standard.
findings.explanation: At the bottom, the hip measured 0.019 shin-lengths below the knee at 2.166 seconds, which is inside the measurement tolerance of 0.03 and too close to call with confidence.

findings.reason: The back is 59 degrees from horizontal at the bottom, toward the vertical end of our +/-15 degree band around the document's 'about 45 degrees'. The document gives a reference posture, not a pass mark, so this is within range rather than exactly correct.
findings.quote: The back angle is formed by the plane of the torso and the floor, which is assumed to be horizontal (meaning level, perpendicular to the force of gravity).
findings.feedback_source: Most people have a picture in their minds of a vertical torso during the squat. The back angle will not be vertical at all; sit back, lean forward, and shove your knees out. Balance problems usually indicate a back angle that is too vertical.
findings.explanation: Your back angle measured 59 degrees from horizontal at the bottom (frame 65, 2.166 s), which falls within the acceptable range around the reference of 45 degrees.

detail.note: Midfoot is the midpoint between heel and toe landmarks.

findings.reason: The bar drifted up to 0.27 shin-lengths from the midfoot, beyond our 0.15 allowance, so it left the balance point during the lift.
findings.quote: So not only is a straight line the shortest distance between two points, but a straight vertical line is also the most efficient bar path for a barbell moving through space in a gravitational framework.
findings.feedback_source: When the bar is off-balance, the added energy you must expend due to the leverage of the off-balance load makes the weight harder to lift. Keep the bar travelling in a vertical line over the middle of the foot through the complete range of motion.
findings.explanation: The bar drifted up to 0.27 shin-lengths away from the midfoot at 2.0 seconds, exceeding the 0.15 shin-length tolerance for a vertical path.
findings.feedback: Keep the bar travelling in a vertical line over the middle of the foot through the complete range of motion. When the bar is off-balance, the added energy you must expend due to the leverage of the off-balance load makes the weight harder to lift.

findings.criterion_name: Hip drive out of the bottom

detail.note: Ratio >= 1 means the hips rose at least as fast as the shoulders.

findings.reason: The shoulders rose faster than the hips out of the bottom (ratio 0.70), which is lifting the chest rather than driving the hips.
findings.quote: come up out of the bottom by driving your butt straight up in the air. Up, not forward.
findings.feedback_source: Think about a chain hooked to your hips, pulling you straight up out of the bottom. Do not think about your knees straightening out, do not think about your feet pushing against the floor. Just drive your hips up out of the bottom.
findings.explanation: Your shoulders rose faster than your hips out of the bottom, with a ratio of 0.70 at 2.166 seconds, meaning you lifted your chest instead of driving your hips straight up.
findings.feedback: Think about a chain hooked to your hips, pulling you straight up out of the bottom. Do not think about your knees straightening out, do not think about your feet pushing against the floor. Just drive your hips up out of the bottom.

summary: Your back angle, knee position at the bottom (sagittal) and heels flat on the floor met the standard on both repetitions. The main thing to fix is bar path over the midfoot, which did not meet the standard on both repetitions (ref p. 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 · Fig 2-5, 2-7). Also short: hip drive out of the bottom. Your squat depth and bar placement on the back landed inside our measurement tolerance, so it was too close to call either way — that is a limit of the measurement, not of the camera angle. We could not measure eye gaze direction in this clip — the evidence was not visible in the frames we needed. Hip drive out of the bottom could not be measured on one repetition, so that verdict covers only part of the set. A side view cannot judge knees shoved out; stance width and toe angle; rack height and unracking procedure at all; those need a different camera angle.
